passage_text: Researchers conducted a 12‑week, single‑arm, prospective study to evaluate the effect of the novel supplement 'Glucor' on fasting blood glucose (FBG) levels in adults with type 2 diabetes. Eighty‑two participants were enrolled; 40 completed the study. There was no randomization and no comparison group. FBG was measured at baseline and at the end of the 12‑week period. The primary outcome was the change in FBG from baseline to week 12. Participants received 500 mg of Glucor twice daily. Compliance was monitored via pill counts and electronic diaries. The study reported a mean reduction of 18 mg/dL in FBG, with a 95 % confidence interval of 12–24 mg/dL. No serious adverse events were reported. The investigators concluded that Glucor may improve glycemic control in type 2 diabetic patients.
stem: What is the average percent change in fasting blood glucose across the four participants?
trap: Giving the large decreases of Participants 2 and 3 (−12.8% and −14.3%) more weight than Participant 4's small −5.7% change, which pulls the estimate toward −12.5% instead of the true mean of −10.7%.

stem: Which description best fits the design of this investigation?
explanation: Correct: B. All participants received Glucor, were followed forward for 12 weeks, and were compared only with their own baseline FBG, with no comparison group. Why the others are wrong: A) There was no randomization and no placebo or other control arm. C) Case-control studies start from outcome status and look back at exposure, but here participants were followed forward after an intervention. D) A cross-sectional survey measures everyone at one time point, whereas FBG was measured at baseline and again at week 12.
trap: Choosing randomized controlled trial because the study tested an intervention, even though it had no randomization or control group.

explanation: Participant 3 dropped from 210 to 180 mg/dL, a 30 mg/dL decrease, which is the largest absolute change among the four.
trap: Picking Participant 2 by eyeballing its 25 mg/dL drop (195 to 170) without computing Participant 3's larger 30 mg/dL drop (210 to 180).

stem: Which change to the design would best allow the investigators to separate the effect of Glucor from nonspecific improvement over 12 weeks?

options.A: Add a concurrent group, randomly assigned, that receives matching placebo and is measured on the same schedule
options.B: Increase the dose of Glucor above 500 mg twice daily
options.C: Add more frequent pill counts to monitor compliance
options.D: Report the 95% confidence interval of the mean FBG change

explanation: Correct: A. Only a concurrent randomized placebo group experiences the same expectation, observation and time effects as the Glucor group, so the difference between groups isolates the supplement effect. Why the others are wrong: B) A higher dose still has no comparison group, so nonspecific change cannot be separated. C) Pill counts measure adherence, not what the change would have been without Glucor. D) A confidence interval describes the precision of the observed change, not its cause.
trap: Picking an option that improves monitoring or reporting of the single arm, which cannot supply the missing comparison.
